hints: Think about what is happening to the charge stored on the capacitor once the switch is closed and how that charge is linked to the p.d. across the capacitor plates.
Think about how the p.d. across the capacitor compares to the p.d. across the resistor in this single loop, and how that p.d. controls the current through the resistor.
Link the discharge current to the rate of loss of charge, and explain why the current falls quickly at first and then more slowly as charge is lost.
walkthrough:
**Start with the charge on the capacitor**
You have a charged capacitor discharging through a resistor. Remember $Q = CV$, so $V_C = Q/C$. As current flows, charge leaves the plates, so $Q$ falls and therefore $V_C$ falls in direct proportion to $Q$.

**Connect capacitor p.d. to resistor current**
There is only one loop, so the p.d. across the resistor must equal the p.d. across the capacitor at every instant: $$V_R = V_C$$ For the resistor, Ohm's law gives $$I = \frac{V_R}{R}$$ So when $V_C$ falls, $V_R$ falls and $I$ falls proportionally.

**Explain why the fall slows down**
The current is the rate at which charge leaves the capacitor: $$I = -\frac{dQ}{dt}$$ At the start $Q$ is large, so $I$ is large and charge is lost quickly. Later $Q$ is small, so $I$ is small and charge is lost slowly. That is why $I$ drops steeply at first and then flattens, the characteristic exponential discharge curve tending to zero.

Final answer: As charge $Q$ decreases, p.d. $V_C = Q/C$ across capacitor decreases. $V_R = V_C$ so current $I = V_R/R$ decreases. Since $I = -dQ/dt$, smaller $I$ means slower loss of charge, so rate of decrease of $I$ decreases, giving exponential decay to zero.

hints: Focus on the instant $t = 0$ in Fig. 6.2. Read off the starting current $I_0$ carefully in $\text{mA}$ and recall what p.d. is driving that current at that instant.
Convert $I_0$ to $\text{A}$ and relate the 12 V initial p.d. to $I_0$ and $R$ to calculate $R$.
walkthrough:
**Read the initial current**
At $t = 0$ the capacitor still has the full $12\text{ V}$ across it, so the resistor also has $12\text{ V}$ across it. From Fig. 6.2 the curve starts at: $$I_0 = 0.13\text{ mA} = 0.13 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A}$$

**Apply Ohm's law at t = 0**
Use: $$R = \frac{V_0}{I_0}$$ $$R = \frac{12}{0.13 \times 10^{-3}} = 9.2 \times 10^4\, \Omega$$ That is about $92\text{ k}\Omega$.

hints: Recall what the time constant $\tau$ means on an $I-t$ discharge graph - it is the time for the initial quantity to fall to a particular fraction of its starting value.
Work out the target current value from your $I_0 = 0.13\text{ mA}$ in (b)(i) and find where that horizontal level meets the curve in Fig. 6.2.
Read off the corresponding time $t$ from the horizontal axis, which equals $\tau$, allowing for small reading tolerance.
walkthrough:
**Use the $1/e$ rule**
For discharge: $$I = I_0 e^{-t/\tau}$$ When $t = \tau$: $$I = I_0 e^{-1} = \frac{I_0}{e}$$ With $I_0 = 0.13\text{ mA}$: $$I = \frac{0.13}{2.718} \approx 0.048\text{ mA}$$

**Read off the graph**
Find $0.048\text{ mA}$ (about $4.8$ small divisions) on the $I$ axis of Fig. 6.2, go across to the curve and down to the $t$ axis. You get: $$t \approx 4.2 \text{ to } 4.4\text{ s}$$

**State the time constant**
That time is the time constant: $$\tau \approx 4.3\text{ s}$$ Any pair of $I,t$ values substituted into the exponential equation gives the same result within reading uncertainty.
Final answer: $I = I_0 e^{-t/\tau}$. When $t = \tau$, $I = I_0/e = 0.13/2.718 = 0.048\text{ mA}$. From Fig. 6.2, $t = 4.3\text{ s}$ when $I = 0.048\text{ mA}$, so $\tau = 4.3\text{ s}$.

hints: Think about how the time constant $\tau$ you found is built from the two circuit components $R$ and $C$.
Rearrange that link to make $C$ the subject and substitute your values of $\tau$ in $\text{s}$ and $R$ in $\Omega$ to get $C$ in $\text{F}$.
walkthrough:
**Link tau, R and C**
For a capacitor-resistor discharge: $$\tau = RC$$ So capacitance is: $$C = \frac{\tau}{R}$$

**Substitute your results**
Using $\tau = 4.3\text{ s}$ and $R = 9.2 \times 10^4\, \Omega$: $$C = \frac{4.3}{9.2 \times 10^4}$$ $$C \approx 4.7 \times 10^{-5}\text{ F}$$ That is about $47\, \mu\text{F}$.
